newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam slams U.S. radio over report on expressway.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam slams U.S. radio over report on expressway.

text.p: Vietnam's Communist Party newspaper blasted the Voice of America (VOA) radio station on Monday for a report on Hanoi's plans to rekindle revolutionary fervour through construction of a new north-south expressway.

"The allegations and distortions, aimed at causing disunity and suspicion, cannot sway the will of each and every Vietnamese person who loves the country and socialism..." the official daily Nhan Dan said.
The commentary also took the U.S. station to task for claiming that the project, whose cost has been put at around $5.5 billion, would be achieved through a compulsory labour programme.

"What do they want when they just go on and on with allegations about 'people being forced to work for free'?" it asked. "They deliberately ignore the reality that building a road or any other construction is an internal affair of every state."
The criticism of VOA comes at a time of improving relations between Vietnam and its former foe, the United States.

Last week the two countries agreed on the text of a bilateral copyright deal, an important step on the way to a comprehensive trade agreement, and next month they are due to exchange ambassadors for the first time.

Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet has championed the expressway plan, saying it would help the economy of remote mountainous regions and take some burden off the existing north-south route, a potholed and flood-prone road known as Highway One.

The grandiose project calls for vast labour teams comprised of youth volunteers and national service conscripts to carve out a route through 1,800 km (1,100 miles) of jungle and mountain terrain down the country's sparsely populated western spine.

Government officials have spoken of millions of workers being involved on a route that will traverse parts of the Ho Chi Minh trail -- a wartime network of paths and roads used to supply ordnance and men from North Vietnam to the South.
However, National Assembly delegates have questioned the viability of the project.

Both Vietnamese and foreign economists have also criticised Kiet's proposal to expand a compulsory labour scheme to build the expressway and other major projects, likening it to discredited labour programmes used by communist governments in the 1950s.
Nhan Dan said the VOA "sounded worried" about the economic benefits of the expressway, which Kiet has said would take 15 years to build.
However, it asked whether VOA was in reality worried about Vietnam becoming a strong country and leaving poverty behind.
